t: 3608 — Minimum Time for K Connected Components
o: Removing all edges with time ≤ t must leave at least k components; find the smallest such t. As t grows, more edges vanish and the component count only increases, so the answer is one of the edge times (or 0 if the initial graph already has ≥ k components). Equivalently: keep edges with time > t; scan edge times in decreasing order, growing the kept graph with DSU, and record the last threshold at which the count was still ≥ k.
k: Component count is monotone non-decreasing in t, so candidates are edge times plus 0.
Processing edges in decreasing-time groups with Union-Find simulates un-removals cleanly, ties included.
Before merging a group of equal time T, the current DSU represents exactly the graph with edges of time > T.

a.i: Sort edges by time descending. Maintain DSU starting with n isolated nodes. For each distinct time T (descending): if the current component count is already ≥ k, then setting t = T works (all edges with time ≤ T are removed and the kept graph — what's built so far — has ≥ k components); record T. Then union all edges of time T. Because we sweep downward, later recorded values are smaller; the final recorded value (or 0 if even the full graph qualifies) is the answer.
s: If the full graph already has ≥ k components, return 0 (checked at the end via the final DSU count).
Sort edges by time descending; init DSU with comp = n, ans = 0.
For each distinct time T: if comp ≥ k set ans = T; then union every edge with time T.
a.t: O(E log E) — sorting dominates; DSU operations are near-linear
a.sp: O(n) for the DSU parent array

a.n: Approach 2: Binary search on t + DSU rebuild
a.i: Since feasibility is monotone in t, binary search t over the sorted distinct edge times (plus 0). Each check rebuilds a DSU from scratch using only edges with time strictly greater than t and compares the component count to k. Simpler to reason about, at the cost of an extra log factor.
s: Collect sorted distinct times; search range [0, maxTime].
check(t): DSU over edges with time > t; return comp ≥ k.
Binary search for the minimal feasible t.
a.t: O(E log E · log T) — each of ~30 checks rebuilds a DSU over all edges
a.sp: O(n) per check for the DSU

w: The descending sweep is optimal and elegant; binary search is the fallback if group/tie handling feels error-prone. Critical pitfall: ties — all edges sharing a time must be removed together, so process them as a group (or rely on strict '>' comparisons in the binary-search version). Also remember t = 0 when the initial graph already has ≥ k components (Example 3).
